cards.q: What is a transition metal?
cards.a: A d-block element that forms one or more stable ions with an incompletely filled d sub-shell (d-orbitals).
cards.why: In Period 4 these are titanium to copper. Their characteristic properties all come from the incomplete \(\mathrm{3d}\) sub-shell.

cards.q: List the four characteristic properties of the transition metals.
cards.a: They form complexes, form coloured ions, show variable oxidation states, and show catalytic activity.
cards.why: All four arise from the incomplete \(\mathrm{d}\) sub-shell.

cards.q: Explain why scandium and zinc are d-block elements but are not transition metals.
cards.a: Their only ions, \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), do not have an incomplete d sub-shell.
marks: Scandium forms only \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\): \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{0}}\), an empty d sub-shell.
Zinc forms only \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\): \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10}}\), a full d sub-shell.
Neither forms a stable ion with an incompletely filled d sub-shell, so neither is a transition metal.

cards.q: True or false: every element in the d-block is a transition metal.
cards.a: False. Scandium and zinc are in the d-block but are not transition metals.
cards.why: A transition metal must form at least one stable ion with an incomplete d sub-shell.

cards.q: Write the electron configuration of a vanadium atom (Z = 23) and of the \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\) ion.
steps: To form \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\), remove the two \(\mathrm{4s}\) electrons, then one \(\mathrm{3d}\) electron: \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{2}}\).
cards.why: Transition metals lose their \(\mathrm{4s}\) electrons before their \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons.

cards.q: Write the electron configuration of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) (Cu: Z = 29).
steps: Cu atom: \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10}\,4s^{1}}\) (a full d sub-shell is more stable).
Remove the \(\mathrm{4s}\) electron first, then one \(\mathrm{3d}\) electron.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{3d^{9}}\) is incomplete, so copper is a transition metal (its \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) ion, \(\mathrm{3d^{10}}\), is not typical).

cards.q: Write the electron configuration of \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) (Cr: Z = 24).
steps: Cr atom: \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{5}\,4s^{1}}\) (a half-filled d sub-shell is more stable).
Remove the \(\mathrm{4s}\) electron, then two \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons.

cards.q: True or false: the electron configuration of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{4}\,4s^{2}}\).
cards.a: False. It is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{6}}\).
cards.why: Fe is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{6}\,4s^{2}}\); the two \(\mathrm{4s}\) electrons are lost first.

cards.q: Explain why transition metals show variable oxidation states (oxidation numbers).
cards.a: The \(\mathrm{4s}\) and \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons have similar energies, so different numbers of them can be lost or used in bonding.
marks: The \(\mathrm{4s}\) and \(\mathrm{3d}\) sub-shells are close in energy.
So successive ionisation energies increase only gradually, with no very large jump across these electrons.
Different numbers of electrons can be lost (or shared), giving ions of similar stability in several oxidation states.

cards.q: Define a ligand.
cards.a: A molecule or ion that forms a co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond with a transition metal by donating a pair of electrons.
cards.why: Every ligand has at least one lone pair of electrons.

cards.q: Define a complex (complex ion).
cards.a: A central metal atom or ion surrounded by ligands.
cards.why: For example \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\): a copper(II) ion surrounded by six water ligands.

cards.q: Define co-ordination number.
cards.a: The number of co-ordinate bonds to the central metal atom or ion.
cards.why: It is not always the number of ligands: a bidentate ligand forms two co-ordinate bonds.

cards.q: Describe the bonding between the copper ion and a water molecule in \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\).
cards.a: A co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond: a lone pair on the oxygen atom is donated to the \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ion.
cards.why: Both electrons in a co-ordinate bond come from the ligand.

cards.q: Explain why \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\), \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) act as monodentate ligands.
cards.a: Each forms only one co-ordinate bond to the metal ion.
marks: Each has a lone pair on one atom (O in \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) and \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\), N in \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\)) that it can donate.
Each forms only one co-ordinate bond to a metal ion (\(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) has two lone pairs, but both are on the same small O atom, so only one can bond to the metal ion).
One co-ordinate bond per ligand means the ligand is monodentate.

cards.q: Give two examples of bidentate ligands and the atoms that donate their lone pairs.
cards.a:
1,2-diaminoethane, \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2}}\) ('en'): the two N atoms.
Ethanedioate, \(\mathrm{C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}}\): two O atoms.
cards.why: A bidentate ligand forms two co-ordinate bonds to the same metal ion.

cards.q: What kind of ligand is \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\), and how many co-ordinate bonds does it form?
cards.a: A multidentate (hexadentate) ligand: it forms six co-ordinate bonds, from two N atoms and four O atoms.
cards.why: One \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\) can occupy all six positions around a metal ion.

cards.q: Give the oxidation state of the metal and the co-ordination number in \(\mathrm{[Cr(C_{2}O_{4})_{3}]^{3-}}\).
cards.a: Chromium is +3; the co-ordination number is 6.
steps: Each ethanedioate is bidentate: \(3 \times 2 = 6\) co-ordinate bonds.
cards.why: Count co-ordinate bonds, not ligands.

cards.q: Give the oxidation state of the metal and the co-ordination number in \(\mathrm{[Cu(EDTA)]^{2-}}\).
cards.a: Copper is +2; the co-ordination number is 6.

cards.q: True or false: the co-ordination number of \(\mathrm{[Ni(H_{2}NCH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2})_{3}]^{2+}}\) is 3, because there are three ligands.
cards.a: False. It is 6: each 1,2-diaminoethane forms two co-ordinate bonds.
cards.why: Co-ordination number counts co-ordinate bonds to the metal, not ligands.

cards.q: Describe the metal complex in haemoglobin and how it carries oxygen.
cards.a: Haem is an iron(II) complex with a multidentate ligand. An \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) molecule forms a co-ordinate bond to the \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ion, so oxygen is carried round the body in the blood.
cards.why: The oxygen binds reversibly, so it can be released in the tissues.

cards.q: Explain why carbon monoxide is toxic.
cards.a: It replaces oxygen bonded to the iron(II) in haemoglobin, so less oxygen is carried.
marks: \(\mathrm{CO}\) is a ligand that forms a co-ordinate bond to the \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) in haemoglobin.
It replaces the \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) ligand: a ligand exchange reaction.
\(\mathrm{CO}\) binds more strongly than \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\), so it is not readily released.
So haemoglobin cannot transport oxygen to cells.

cards.q: What shape is \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\), and what is the bond angle?
cards.a: Octahedral, with bond angles of \(90^{\circ}\).
cards.why: Small ligands such as \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) usually give six-co-ordinate, octahedral complexes.

cards.q: Explain why a complex with six co-ordinate bonds is octahedral.
cards.a: Six bonding pairs repel each other equally and get as far apart as possible.
marks: There are six pairs of electrons in co-ordinate bonds around the metal ion.
These electron pairs repel each other equally.
They get as far apart as possible: an octahedral arrangement with \(90^{\circ}\) bond angles.

cards.q: Why is \(\mathrm{[CuCl_{4}]^{2-}}\) tetrahedral and not octahedral? Give its bond angle.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ligands are large, so only four fit around the metal ion. Four bonding pairs repel to a tetrahedral shape, \(109.5^{\circ}\).
cards.why: Larger ligands such as \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) commonly give tetrahedral complexes.

cards.q: Name the shape of cisplatin, \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_{3})_{2}Cl_{2}]}\), and give its bond angle.
cards.a: Square planar, \(90^{\circ}\).
cards.why: Square planar complexes have four co-ordinate bonds in one plane, unlike tetrahedral complexes.

cards.q: Give the shape and bond angle of the complex in Tollens' reagent, \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+}}\).
cards.a: Linear, \(180^{\circ}\).
cards.why: Two co-ordinate bonds from \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) to \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\) get as far apart as possible.

cards.q: Describe the cis and trans isomers of the octahedral complex \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_{3})_{4}Cl_{2}]^{+}}\).
cards.a:
Cis: the two \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ligands are next to each other, at \(90^{\circ}\).
Trans: the two \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ligands are opposite each other, at \(180^{\circ}\).
cards.why: Octahedral complexes of the type \(\mathrm{[MA_{4}B_{2}]}\) with monodentate ligands show cis–trans isomerism (a special case of E–Z isomerism).

cards.q: Which type of stereoisomerism does \(\mathrm{[Ni(H_{2}NCH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2})_{3}]^{2+}}\) show, and why?
cards.a: Optical isomerism: the complex exists as two non-superimposable mirror images.
cards.why: Octahedral complexes with three bidentate ligands are chiral, like a three-bladed propeller twisted one way or the other.

cards.q: What is cisplatin, and how does it work as an anticancer drug?
cards.a: The cis isomer of square planar \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_{3})_{2}Cl_{2}]}\). It binds to DNA in cancer cells (the two \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ligands are replaced by nitrogen atoms on the DNA), which stops the DNA replicating, so the cells cannot divide.
cards.why: It also affects healthy cells, so it has side effects such as hair loss.

cards.q: Explain why cisplatin is supplied as a single isomer and not mixed with the trans isomer.
cards.a: Only the cis isomer binds to DNA in the way that makes it work; the trans isomer is not effective and may cause harm.
marks: In the cis isomer the two Cl ligands are next to each other, so it can bond to two neighbouring sites on DNA.
The trans isomer has a different shape and cannot bind to DNA in the same way, so it is not effective.
Including the trans isomer would reduce the effective dose and could cause different, unwanted (toxic) side effects.

cards.q: True or false: tetrahedral complexes such as \(\mathrm{[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}}\) can show cis–trans isomerism, like square planar ones.
cards.a: False. In a tetrahedron every position is next to every other, so there is no cis or trans arrangement.
cards.why: Cis–trans isomerism is shown by square planar and octahedral complexes.

cards.q: Why does replacing \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) ligands with \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) ligands not change the co-ordination number?
cards.a: \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) are similar in size and both uncharged.
cards.why: So six of either fit around the metal ion, and the complex stays octahedral.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) with excess concentrated ammonia, and give the colour change.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} + 6NH_{3} \rightarrow [Co(NH_{3})_{6}]^{2+} + 6H_{2}O}\)
Pink solution to straw-coloured (pale yellow-brown) solution.
cards.why: The co-ordination number stays at 6. The ammine complex darkens in air as it is oxidised to cobalt(III).

cards.q: Write the overall equation for \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) reacting with excess ammonia, and give the colour change.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} + 4NH_{3} \rightarrow [Cu(NH_{3})_{4}(H_{2}O)_{2}]^{2+} + 4H_{2}O}\)
Blue solution to deep (dark) blue solution.
cards.why: Substitution is incomplete: only four of the six water ligands are replaced.

cards.q: Describe what is seen, step by step, as aqueous ammonia is added dropwise to copper(II) sulfate solution until in excess.
cards.a: A pale blue precipitate of \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}]}\) forms first; it then dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep blue solution of \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_{3})_{4}(H_{2}O)_{2}]^{2+}}\).
cards.why: A little ammonia acts as a base; excess ammonia acts as a ligand, replacing \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\).

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) with concentrated hydrochloric acid, and give the colour change.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} + 4Cl^{-} \rightleftharpoons [CuCl_{4}]^{2-} + 6H_{2}O}\)
Blue solution to yellow (or yellow-green) solution.
cards.why: The co-ordination number changes from 6 to 4 and the shape from octahedral to tetrahedral. A mixture of the two complexes looks green.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) with concentrated hydrochloric acid, and give the colour change.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} + 4Cl^{-} \rightleftharpoons [CoCl_{4}]^{2-} + 6H_{2}O}\)
Pink solution to blue solution.
cards.why: Octahedral (co-ordination number 6) to tetrahedral (co-ordination number 4).

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) with concentrated hydrochloric acid.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+} + 4Cl^{-} \rightleftharpoons [FeCl_{4}]^{-} + 6H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Another example where the larger chloride ligand reduces the co-ordination number from 6 to 4.

cards.q: Explain why the co-ordination number changes when \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) ligands are replaced by \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ligands.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) is larger than \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) (and charged), so fewer fit around the metal ion.
marks: \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ligands are larger than uncharged \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) ligands.
Being negatively charged, the \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ligands also repel each other more.
Only four fit around the metal ion, so the co-ordination number falls from 6 to 4 (octahedral to tetrahedral).

cards.q: True or false: when concentrated HCl is added to \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\), the product is the octahedral complex \(\mathrm{[CuCl_{6}]^{4-}}\).
cards.a: False. The product is tetrahedral \(\mathrm{[CuCl_{4}]^{2-}}\).
cards.why: Six large \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ligands do not fit around the copper ion.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) with \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\), and state how many particles there are on each side.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} + EDTA^{4-} \rightarrow [Cu(EDTA)]^{2-} + 6H_{2}O}\)
2 particles become 7.
cards.why: The increase in the number of particles gives a large increase in entropy.

cards.q: Explain the chelate effect: why bidentate and multidentate ligands replace monodentate ligands.
cards.a: The substitution greatly increases the number of particles, so entropy increases, while the enthalpy change is close to zero.
marks: For example, \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} + 3H_{2}NCH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2} \rightarrow [Cu(H_{2}NCH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2})_{3}]^{2+} + 6H_{2}O}\): 4 particles become 7.
So there is a large increase in entropy: \(\Delta S\) is positive.
Similar bonds (co-ordinate bonds to the metal) are broken and made, so \(\Delta H\) is approximately zero.
So \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) is negative: the reaction is feasible and the chelate complex is more stable.

cards.q: A ligand substitution in which a hexadentate ligand replaces six water ligands has \(\Delta H = -2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S = +150\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\). Calculate \(\Delta G\) at 298 K.
cards.a: \(-46.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Almost all of the driving force comes from the entropy term, \(T\Delta S\).

cards.q: True or false: EDTA complexes are more stable than aqua complexes mainly because the bonds EDTA forms to the metal are much stronger.
cards.a: False. The bonds are similar in strength; the enthalpy change is close to zero.
cards.why: The chelate effect is driven by the large increase in entropy as more particles are released.

cards.q: Explain why transition metal complexes are coloured.
cards.a: Ligands split the d orbitals into two energy levels; d electrons absorb visible light to move to the higher level, and the light not absorbed is seen.
marks: Ligands cause the d orbitals to split into levels of different energy.
A d electron absorbs a photon of visible light and moves from the ground state to an excited state (higher d level).
The energy absorbed matches the gap: \(\Delta E = h\nu\).
Some wavelengths are absorbed; the remaining wavelengths are transmitted or reflected, and this is the colour seen.

cards.q: Write the equation linking the energy gap between split d orbitals to the frequency and wavelength of light absorbed.
cards.a: \(\Delta E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)
cards.why: \(h\) is the Planck constant, \(\nu\) the frequency, \(c\) the speed of light and \(\lambda\) the wavelength. A bigger gap means higher frequency, shorter wavelength.

cards.q: A complex absorbs light of wavelength 500 nm. Calculate the energy gap between its d orbitals, per ion. (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(3.98 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\)
cards.why: Always convert nanometres to metres first.

cards.q: The d-orbital splitting in a complex is \(199\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Calculate the wavelength of light it absorbs, in nm. (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\), \(L = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.a: 602 nm
cards.why: Divide the molar energy by the Avogadro constant to get the energy for one ion, and convert kJ to J.

cards.q: True or false: a transition metal solution appears green because it absorbs green light.
cards.a: False. It looks green because green light is transmitted (not absorbed); it absorbs other wavelengths.
cards.why: We see the wavelengths that pass through or are reflected.

cards.q: Explain why \(\mathrm{[Sc(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Zn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) are colourless.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) has no d electrons (\(\mathrm{3d^{0}}\)) and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) has a full d sub-shell (\(\mathrm{3d^{10}}\)), so no d electron can move to a higher d level.
marks: \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{0}}\): there are no d electrons to promote.
\(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10}}\): the upper d level is full, so no electron can move into it.
So no visible light is absorbed by d-electron transitions, and the solutions are colourless.

cards.q: Apart from having an empty or full d sub-shell, why might a complex ion be colourless?
cards.a: The energy gap between the split d orbitals may be too large, so the light absorbed is in the ultraviolet, not the visible region.
cards.why: If no visible wavelengths are absorbed, all visible light is transmitted and the solution looks colourless.

cards.q: What three changes to a complex alter \(\Delta E\) and so change its colour? Give an example of each.
cards.a:
Oxidation state: \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) (pale green) to \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}}\) (solutions look yellow-brown).
Ligand: \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) (blue) to \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_{3})_{4}(H_{2}O)_{2}]^{2+}}\) (deep blue).
Co-ordination number: \(\mathrm{[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\) (pink) to \(\mathrm{[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}}\) (blue).
cards.why: Each change alters the size of the d-orbital splitting, so a different wavelength is absorbed.

cards.q: Describe how a colorimeter is used to find the concentration of a solution of coloured ions.
cards.a: Make up standard solutions of known concentration, measure their absorbance and plot a calibration graph; measure the absorbance of the unknown and read its concentration off the graph.
cards.why: Use a filter (wavelength) of the colour the ions absorb most strongly. A ligand such as ammonia can be added to intensify a pale colour.

cards.q: A calibration graph for copper(II) ions is a straight line through the origin with a gradient of \(2.80\ \text{dm}^{3}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\). An unknown solution has an absorbance of 0.420. Find its concentration.
cards.a: \(0.150\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: The unknown must lie within the range of the standards for the reading to be reliable.

cards.q: Give the colours of vanadium in its +5, +4, +3 and +2 oxidation states in aqueous solution.
cards.a:
+5, \(\mathrm{VO_{2}^{+}}\): yellow.
+4, \(\mathrm{VO^{2+}}\): blue.
+3, \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\): green.
+2, \(\mathrm{V^{2+}}\): violet (purple).
cards.why: A mnemonic: "You Better Get Vanadium" (yellow, blue, green, violet), going down in oxidation state.

cards.q: Describe the colour changes when zinc is added to an acidified solution of ammonium vanadate(V).
cards.a: Yellow, then green, then blue, then green, then violet.
cards.why: The first green is a mixture of yellow (+5) and blue (+4); the second green is vanadium(III). Zinc reduces vanadium all the way to +2.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reduction of \(\mathrm{VO_{2}^{+}}\) to \(\mathrm{VO^{2+}}\) by zinc in acid.
cards.why: Each vanadium goes from +5 to +4 (one electron each); each zinc gives two electrons.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reduction of \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\) to \(\mathrm{V^{2+}}\) by zinc.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{2V^{3+} + Zn \rightarrow 2V^{2+} + Zn^{2+}}\)
cards.why: Green to violet. The \(\mathrm{V^{2+}}\) is easily re-oxidised by air, so the flask is loosely stoppered.

cards.q: Use \(E^{\ominus}\) values to show that zinc can reduce \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\) to \(\mathrm{V^{2+}}\). (\(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}\): −0.76 V; \(\mathrm{V^{3+}/V^{2+}}\): −0.26 V)
cards.a: \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.50\ \text{V}\), which is positive, so the reaction is feasible.
cards.why: Zinc's \(E^{\ominus}\) is more negative than all three vanadium couples, so it reduces vanadium all the way to +2.

cards.q: Can iodide ions reduce \(\mathrm{VO_{2}^{+}}\) to \(\mathrm{VO^{2+}}\), and then \(\mathrm{VO^{2+}}\) to \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\)? (\(\mathrm{I_{2}/I^{-}}\): +0.54 V; \(\mathrm{VO_{2}^{+}/VO^{2+}}\): +1.00 V; \(\mathrm{VO^{2+}/V^{3+}}\): +0.34 V)
cards.a: Yes to \(\mathrm{VO^{2+}}\) (\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = +0.46\ \text{V}\)); no further (\(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = -0.20\ \text{V}\)). The reduction stops at vanadium(IV), blue.
cards.why: A reducing agent can only reduce a species whose couple has a more positive \(E^{\ominus}\) than its own.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reduction of dichromate(VI) ions to chromium(III) by zinc in acid, and give the colour change.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-} + 14H^{+} + 3Zn \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 3Zn^{2+} + 7H_{2}O}\)
Orange to green.
cards.why: Each chromium goes from +6 to +3: six electrons for two Cr, supplied by three Zn.

cards.q: Zinc in acid reduces \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) further. Give the product, its colour, and the \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}\). (\(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr^{2+}}\): −0.41 V; \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}\): −0.76 V)
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\), blue. \(E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}} = -0.41 - (-0.76) = +0.35\ \text{V}\), so feasible.
cards.why: Air must be kept out: \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is readily oxidised back to green \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) by oxygen.

cards.q: Describe how chromium(III) ions are converted into dichromate(VI) ions, with the colour at each stage.
cards.a: Add excess sodium hydroxide (dark green solution of \(\mathrm{[Cr(OH)_{6}]^{3-}}\)), then hydrogen peroxide and warm: yellow chromate(VI), \(\mathrm{CrO_{4}^{2-}}\). Then acidify: orange dichromate(VI), \(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}}\).
cards.why: Chromium(III) is far easier to oxidise in alkaline conditions than in acid. Excess hydrogen peroxide is boiled off before acidifying, or it would reduce the dichromate(VI).

cards.q: Write the equation for the oxidation of \(\mathrm{[Cr(OH)_{6}]^{3-}}\) by hydrogen peroxide in alkaline solution.
cards.why: Chromium goes from +3 to +6; oxygen in hydrogen peroxide goes from −1 to −2.

cards.q: Explain why transition metal ions in a low oxidation state are more easily oxidised in alkaline solution than in acidic solution.
cards.a: The half-equation for reducing the higher oxidation state uses up \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ions, so its electrode potential falls as the pH rises.
marks: The reduction of the higher oxidation state uses \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), e.g. \(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-} + 14H^{+} + 6e^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_{2}O}\).
Lowering the concentration of H⁺ moves this equilibrium to the left, so the electrode potential becomes less positive.
The higher oxidation state is a weaker oxidising agent, so the lower oxidation state is more easily oxidised.
The ligand matters too: in alkali the metal is bound to \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) instead of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\), which also changes the potential.

cards.q: Write the equilibrium between chromate(VI) and dichromate(VI) ions, and give their colours.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{2CrO_{4}^{2-} + 2H^{+} \rightleftharpoons Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-} + H_{2}O}\)
Chromate(VI): yellow. Dichromate(VI): orange.
cards.why: Adding acid moves the equilibrium right (orange); adding alkali removes H⁺ and moves it left (yellow).

cards.q: True or false: the conversion of yellow chromate(VI) into orange dichromate(VI) by acid is a redox reaction.
cards.a: False. Chromium is +6 in both ions; it is an acid–base equilibrium.

cards.q: How is Tollens' reagent, \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+}}\), used to distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone?
cards.a: Warm the compound with Tollens' reagent. An aldehyde reduces the silver(I) complex to metallic silver, giving a silver mirror; a ketone gives no change.
cards.why: Half-equation: \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow Ag + 2NH_{3}}\). The aldehyde is oxidised to a carboxylic acid (carboxylate).

cards.q: Write the half-equation for manganate(VII) acting as an oxidising agent in acid, and the overall equation for its reaction with \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\).
cards.why: Mole ratio \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-} : Fe^{2+}}\) is \(1 : 5\).

cards.q: Write the overall equation for the reaction of acidified manganate(VII) with ethanedioate ions.
cards.why: Ethanedioate half-equation: \(\mathrm{C_{2}O_{4}^{2-} \rightarrow 2CO_{2} + 2e^{-}}\). Mole ratio \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-} : C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}}\) is \(2 : 5\).

cards.q: In a titration with potassium manganate(VII), how is the end point seen, and why is no indicator needed?
cards.a: The end point is the first permanent pale pink colour in the flask.
cards.why: Before the end point, purple \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) is decolourised as it is reduced to almost colourless \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\); the first excess drop stays pink. Read the top of the meniscus, as the solution is too dark to see the bottom.

cards.q: Why is a manganate(VII) titration acidified with dilute sulfuric acid, and not hydrochloric, nitric or ethanoic acid?
cards.a: Sulfuric acid supplies plenty of H⁺ without reacting with the manganate(VII) or the sample.
marks: Hydrochloric acid: \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) by \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\), so too much manganate(VII) is used (titre too high).
Nitric acid is itself an oxidising agent, so it would oxidise \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) and the titre would be too low.
Ethanoic acid is a weak acid: too little \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), so brown \(\mathrm{MnO_{2}}\) forms instead of \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\).

cards.q: An iron tablet is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and made up to \(250\ \text{cm}^{3}\). A \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) portion needs \(12.40\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.0100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{KMnO_{4}}\). Calculate the mass of iron in the tablet. (\(A_{\text{r}}\): Fe 55.8)
cards.a: 0.346 g
cards.why: Remember the 1 : 5 ratio and to scale up from the portion titrated to the whole solution.

cards.q: 9.80 g of hydrated ammonium iron(II) sulfate is dissolved and made up to \(250\ \text{cm}^{3}\). \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of this needs \(25.00\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.0200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{KMnO_{4}}\). Calculate the \(M_{\text{r}}\) of the salt.
cards.a: 392
steps: Each formula unit contains one \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), so \(M_{\text{r}} = \dfrac{9.80}{0.0250} = 392\)
cards.why: This matches \(\mathrm{(NH_{4})_{2}Fe(SO_{4})_{2}{\cdot}6H_{2}O}\).

cards.q: 1.575 g of hydrated ethanedioic acid, \(\mathrm{H_{2}C_{2}O_{4}{\cdot}xH_{2}O}\), is made up to \(250\ \text{cm}^{3}\). \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) needs \(25.00\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.0200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{KMnO_{4}}\) at about 60 °C. Find \(x\). (\(M_{\text{r}}\) of \(\mathrm{H_{2}C_{2}O_{4}}\) = 90.0)
cards.a: \(x = 2\)

cards.q: \(10.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of hair bleach is diluted to \(250\ \text{cm}^{3}\). \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) needs \(22.40\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.0200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{KMnO_{4}}\). Given \(\mathrm{2MnO_{4}^{-} + 6H^{+} + 5H_{2}O_{2} \rightarrow 2Mn^{2+} + 8H_{2}O + 5O_{2}}\), find the concentration of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O_{2}}\) in the bleach.
cards.a: \(1.12\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: The dilution factor is 25: every mole titrated came from a twenty-fifth of the original bleach.

cards.q: \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of an \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) solution needs \(18.60\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.0200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Given \(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-} + 14H^{+} + 6Fe^{2+} \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_{2}O + 6Fe^{3+}}\), find the concentration of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\).
cards.a: \(0.0893\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\)
cards.why: Each dichromate(VI) ion accepts six electrons: two Cr atoms each going from +6 to +3.

cards.q: Define a heterogeneous catalyst and a homogeneous catalyst.
cards.a:
Heterogeneous: in a different phase from the reactants; the reaction happens at active sites on its surface.
Homogeneous: in the same phase as the reactants; the reaction goes via an intermediate species.
cards.why: Iron in the Haber process is heterogeneous (solid catalyst, gaseous reactants); aqueous Fe²⁺ with aqueous reactants is homogeneous.

cards.q: Explain why variable oxidation states make transition metals good catalysts.
cards.a: The metal can gain and lose electrons easily, so it can take part in redox steps and be regenerated, giving a route with a lower activation energy.
marks: The metal ion can change easily between oxidation states.
So it can accept electrons from one reactant and pass them to another (or form intermediates).
It is regenerated in its original oxidation state at the end.
This provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy.

cards.q: Describe the three stages by which a heterogeneous catalyst works.
cards.a: Adsorption of reactant molecules onto active sites on the surface; weakening of bonds and reaction; desorption of the product molecules from the surface.
cards.why: The surface holds the reactants close together in a favourable orientation, and the weakened bonds lower the activation energy.

cards.q: Why is a heterogeneous catalyst often spread thinly on a support medium, such as the ceramic honeycomb in a catalytic converter?
cards.a: To maximise the surface area of catalyst and minimise the amount (and so the cost) of the expensive metal used.
cards.why: Only the surface atoms take part in catalysis.

cards.q: Explain what is meant by catalyst poisoning and why it matters in industry.
cards.a: Impurities adsorb onto the active sites and block them, so the catalyst becomes less efficient.
marks: Impurities are strongly adsorbed onto (block) the active sites on the surface.
Fewer active sites are available for reactants, so the catalyst is less efficient.
This has a cost: the catalyst must be replaced or regenerated, or the reactants purified first (e.g. sulfur impurities poison the iron catalyst in the Haber process).

cards.q: Which transition metal catalyses the Haber process, and what type of catalyst is it?
cards.a: Iron, a heterogeneous catalyst: \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\).
cards.why: The solid iron is in a different phase from the gaseous reactants.

cards.q: Explain, with equations, how vanadium(V) oxide catalyses the Contact process, \(\mathrm{2SO_{2} + O_{2} \rightarrow 2SO_{3}}\).
cards.a: \(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{5}}\) oxidises \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) and is reduced; oxygen then re-oxidises it, so it is regenerated.
marks: \(\mathrm{SO_{2} + V_{2}O_{5} \rightarrow SO_{3} + V_{2}O_{4}}\): vanadium is reduced from +5 to +4.
\(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{4} + \tfrac{1}{2}O_{2} \rightarrow V_{2}O_{5}}\): vanadium is oxidised back from +4 to +5.
\(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{5}}\) is regenerated, so it is a catalyst; this works because vanadium has variable oxidation states.
It is heterogeneous: solid \(\mathrm{V_{2}O_{5}}\), gaseous reactants.

cards.q: Explain how a catalytic converter removes carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide from car exhaust.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{2CO + 2NO \rightarrow 2CO_{2} + N_{2}}\) on the surface of a platinum/rhodium catalyst.
marks: \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{NO}\) molecules are adsorbed onto the surface of the catalyst.
Bonds in the adsorbed molecules are weakened and they react.
The products, \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\), are desorbed from the surface.

cards.q: Explain, with equations, how \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ions catalyse the reaction between \(\mathrm{S_{2}O_{8}^{2-}}\) and \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\).
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is oxidised by peroxodisulfate and then reduced back by iodide, so two reactions between oppositely charged ions replace one between negative ions.
marks: Uncatalysed: \(\mathrm{S_{2}O_{8}^{2-} + 2I^{-} \rightarrow 2SO_{4}^{2-} + I_{2}}\) is slow because two negative ions repel, so the activation energy is high.
\(\mathrm{2Fe^{3+} + 2I^{-} \rightarrow 2Fe^{2+} + I_{2}}\)
Each step is between oppositely charged ions, so it has a lower activation energy; \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is regenerated.

cards.q: Explain, with equations, how \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ions autocatalyse the reaction between \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}}\).
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is a product that catalyses the reaction, via \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\).
marks: \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is a product of the reaction and also its catalyst (autocatalysis).
The uncatalysed reaction is slow at first because the reactant ions are both negative and repel.

cards.q: Describe how the rate of reaction between acidified \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}}\) changes as the reaction proceeds.
cards.a: Slow at first, then speeds up as \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) (the catalyst) builds up, then slows down as the reactants are used up.
cards.why: A graph of [MnO₄⁻] against time is S-shaped (it starts flat, then falls steeply, then levels off). In a titration the first drops decolourise slowly, then quickly.

cards.q: True or false: the reaction between \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{C_{2}O_{4}^{2-}}\) speeds up after it starts because the mixture warms up.
cards.a: False (as the main reason). It speeds up because the product \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is a catalyst.
cards.why: This is autocatalysis: the rate rises as the concentration of catalyst rises.
